extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, advocates, nonprofits, businesses, and practitioners who want to submit comments on U.S. federal regulations
extracted.subtask_short: writing public comments on federal regulations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting effective notice-and-comment submissions to U.S. federal agencies, emphasizing evidence, specificity, and procedural steps (where to find the rule, what documents to read, how to cite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness principle: facts/evidence/insights
rubrics_metrics.description: "Comments influence rules only to the extent that they bring forth relevant facts, evidence, and insights to rule makers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central evaluative principle: submissions are persuasive when they supply relevant factual material and analytic insights into the specific proposal rather than mere expressions of support or opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant facts and data
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide relevant facts and data supporting your position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, domain-specific facts (data, statistics, case examples) that directly bear on the rule's effects or the agency's analyses. Avoid unsupported assertions or anecdote-only arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based arguments (not general opinions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer evidence-based arguments rather than general opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite studies, empirical analyses, regulatory impact analyses, or other verifiable evidence. Anti-pattern: broad moralizing or unsupported claims that add little to the agency's factual record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive insights addressing the specific proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide substantive insights that address the specific proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how the proposed rule would operate in practice, who it would affect, unintended consequences, implementation challenges, or alternative approaches. Tailor comments to the actual text and intent of the proposal rather than speaking only in abstract principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit within the comment period (timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory agencies typically open comment periods of 30-60 days after announcing a proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File comments during the official notice-and-comment window; late submissions may be excluded unless the agency reopens the record. Monitor the Federal Register or regulations.gov for deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate rule on regulations.gov or federalregister.gov
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the proposed rule on regulations.gov or federalregister.gov before drafting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the official docket page to view the proposal, supporting documents, and other public submissions. This is the primary platform agencies use to collect and organize comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the agency's preamble and supporting analytical documents (RIA, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the agency's preamble and supporting analytical documents (RIA, etc.) before drafting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the agency's stated rationale, legal basis, and quantitative analyses so your comment can identify errors, gaps, or alternative evidence. Referencing the agency's own documents strengthens credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address specific sections and cite Federal Register pagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Address specific sections; cite Federal Register pagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directly point to regulatory text, provisions, or page citations in the Federal Register so reviewers can locate the passage you discuss. Specificity (e.g., section numbers, FR page) increases usefulness to agency staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your comment self-contained; focus on substance not signaling
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your comment self-contained — agencies score on substance, not signaling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the submission includes enough explanation and evidence on its own; do not rely solely on external links or symbolic gestures. Agencies prioritize substantive contributions that modify the administrative record over mere expressions of support/opposition.
